idiom_name: application service class registered with the built-in DI container (AddScoped) and an EF Core transaction as the unit of work
implementation_notes: In ASP.NET Core the platform supplies what the EJB container used to: register the coarse class with AddScoped (one instance per request) or AddTransient, and inject the fine-grained collaborators through the constructor - the built-in IServiceProvider resolves the graph and disposes scoped services at the end of the scope. What still has to be written by hand is the coarse class itself; what replaces the container-managed transaction is an explicit unit of work, typically await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync() around the workflow, or TransactionScope when several resources must enlist. Choose the explicit application-service class over inlining orchestration in minimal-API handlers whenever several entry points (controllers, background services, gRPC services) share the same workflow or the transaction boundary must be visible in one place.
pitfalls: Injecting a scoped DbContext into a singleton facade (or into a BackgroundService constructor) fails with 'Cannot consume scoped service from singleton'; create an explicit scope with IServiceScopeFactory.CreateScope() instead.

Resolving collaborators from IServiceProvider inside the facade hides the dependency graph and defeats container validation (ValidateOnBuild/ValidateScopes), which is exactly the safety net the container provides.
TransactionScope escalates to a distributed transaction when a second connection enlists; for a single database prefer the explicit DbContext transaction, and never await unrelated I/O inside it.
